newsitem.title: UK: EMERGING MARKET OUTLOOK - Czech poll, Ivorian debt.
newsitem.headline: EMERGING MARKET OUTLOOK - Czech poll, Ivorian debt.

text.p: Senate elections in the Czech Republic and a debt restructuring deal for the Ivory Coast will broaden the focus of emerging market investors over the coming week.

After a week driven primarily by news from Russia amid the launch of its debut Eurobond, and an absence of news from the Latin American giants, investors will be looking further afield for market moving news.
The three-party coalition of right-wing Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus won a majority of seats on Saturday in run-off elections to parliament's new upper house.
After weeks in the doldrums, the Czech stock market rallied in advance of the result, also buoying the Czech crown against its dollar/mark basket in the process.
The markets had expected the vote to give a filip to Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, but politics in the republic will remain as intractable as ever.

"The likely outcome will preserve Klaus's position in the ODS (Civic Democratic Party) but it doesn't make policymaking any easier," said David Lubin, economic advisor for emerging markets at HSBC in London, pointing to deadlock in the lower house after the ODS lost its majority in mid-year polls.
But he said the Czechs' problems paled into insignificance compared with those in BULGARIA.
"Bulgaria is facing the spectre of default," another analyst said, adding investors were hoping for word about setting up an IMF-proposed currency board this week.

The Bulgarian lev has collapsed and hyperinflation looms in the absence of IMF funds which are conditional on reforming the economy. The Fund has recommended the creation of a monetary board to stabilise the economy but confusion over its impact sparked panic selling of the lev last week.
Though Sofia may be able to pay January's semi-annual coupon on its outstanding debt, prospects beyond that look bleak.

The IVORY COAST will be keeping fixed income investors glued to their calculators after it reached agreement last week with the London Club to create new Brady-style bonds out of $7.2 billion in outstanding commercial debt.
"The banks and the Ivorians were very far apart and people hadn't expected the deal to be completed so quickly," said Dan McGovern, head of emerging markets fixed income research at Merrill Lynch.

"There will be lots of activity as people try to value the bonds -- people are only just starting to calculate them now," he said. On Friday he saw only bids and no offers on the unrestructured Ivorian loans, with everyone wanting to buy.
Other investors will be watching the SOUTH AFRICAN rand after last week's 100 basis discount rate increase.
"It will be very interesting to watch the rand -- it is a bit odd that it has appreciated so strongly and there is still a lot of vulnerability in the currency," HSBC's Lubin said.
Latin American markets were expected to remain mainly quiet this week, with attention focused on a raft of U.S. data.
Some investors said they would be looking out for volatility in MEXICO after the emergence of a new guerrilla group there, but others said there was no reason for nerves.
"It looks like a flash in the pan," said Yxa Bazan, Latin American analyst at Indosuez Capital Research. "The currency is the first indicator of any worry and that's remained stable."
Middle Eastern investors will be watching LEBANON after recent comments from the central bank that it would like to see Treasury bill yields fall.

"Investors should be worried if interest rates fall too low -- they should not be reducing interest rates by more than 50 basis points unless the government makes a demonstrable commitment to tightening the budget," HSBC's Lubin said.
The IFC composite index of emerging market equities, denominated in dollars IFC/IPRD, was up 0.4 percent at 294.36 points on Friday compared with a week ago.
Latin America was down 0.7 percent week-on-week at 527.62, Asia was up 0.6 at 253.90, and Europe, Middle East and Africa was up 1.8 percent at 135.68. --London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
